cloud-concepts.title: Cloud Concepts

sections.heading: What Is Cloud Computing?
sections.body: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, and software — over the internet, on demand, from a provider like Microsoft Azure. Instead of buying and maintaining physical hardware in your own building, you rent exactly the capacity you need and pay only for what you use. This is a fundamental shift from capital expenditure (CapEx) — a large upfront purchase of hardware that then sits there whether you use it or not — to operational expenditure (OpEx), where cost tracks actual consumption.

sections.heading: Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
sections.body: Azure offers three main service models, distinguished by how much of the technology stack you manage versus how much Microsoft manages for you. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) — for example, an Azure Virtual Machine — hands you a virtual machine and lets you manage the operating system, runtime, and applications yourself. Platform as a Service (PaaS) — for example, Azure App Service — takes the operating system and runtime off your plate so you can focus purely on your application code and data. Software as a Service (SaaS) — for example, Microsoft 365 — is a complete, ready-to-use application; you just sign in and use it. As you move from IaaS toward SaaS, you trade control for convenience: Microsoft manages progressively more of the stack.

sections.heading: The Shared Responsibility Model
sections.body: No matter which service model you use, security and management responsibilities are shared between you and Microsoft — and where that line falls shifts depending on the model. The one constant across every model, including SaaS, is that you always retain responsibility for your data, your devices, and your accounts and identities. Microsoft never takes that part over for you. The diagram below shows exactly how the rest of the responsibility shifts as you move from on-premises infrastructure through IaaS and PaaS to SaaS.

sections.heading: Cloud Deployment Models: Public, Private, and Hybrid
sections.body: Public cloud means the infrastructure is owned and operated by a third-party provider (like Microsoft) and shared across many customers over the internet — this is what most people mean by 'the cloud,' and it's what Azure itself is. Private cloud means the infrastructure is dedicated to a single organization, often for stricter regulatory, compliance, or customization needs. Hybrid cloud combines the two: some workloads run on-premises or in a private cloud, others run in the public cloud, connected together. Organizations often choose hybrid when they have legacy systems that can't easily move, or data residency rules that require certain data to stay on-premises, while still wanting the scalability of the public cloud for everything else. Don't confuse hybrid cloud with multi-cloud — using two or more public cloud providers together — which is a different concept entirely.

sections.heading: Why Organizations Move to the Cloud
sections.body: Cloud computing offers several benefits that are difficult or expensive to achieve on-premises. High availability means designing systems with redundancy so they keep running even if individual components fail. Scalability is the ability to increase or decrease resource capacity — either vertically (a bigger VM) or horizontally (more VMs). Elasticity goes a step further: resources automatically scale up or down in response to real-time demand, without manual intervention, so you're never paying for idle capacity or getting caught short during a spike. Agility is the speed at which you can provision, test, and deploy new solutions. And because large providers like Microsoft operate at massive scale, they can offer better economies of scale — generally lower per-unit costs — than most organizations could achieve running their own datacenter.

keyTakeaways: Cloud computing delivers IT resources on demand over the internet, billed on a consumption (OpEx) basis instead of a large upfront (CapEx) purchase.

IaaS gives you the most control (you manage the OS upward), PaaS lets Microsoft manage the runtime and OS so you focus on your application, and SaaS is a ready-to-use application you don't manage at all.
Under the shared responsibility model, you always retain responsibility for your data, devices, and identities — no matter which service model you use.
Public cloud is fully hosted by a third-party provider; private cloud is dedicated to one organization; hybrid cloud combines both, often for compliance or legacy-system reasons.
Scalability (adding or removing capacity) and elasticity (automatically adjusting capacity to match real-time demand) are related but distinct concepts.

High availability and disaster recovery both aim to keep systems running, but high availability is about tolerating failures with minimal disruption, while disaster recovery is about restoring service after a major outage.
examTips: AZ-900 loves scenario questions like "a company wants X — which service or deployment model fits?" Practice mapping keywords (e.g. "regulatory data residency" → private or hybrid) to the right answer rather than memorizing definitions in isolation.

Memorize the shared responsibility rule "data and identity are always yours" — it's one of the most frequently tested single facts in this entire domain, and it resurfaces in the Identity and Security modules too.
Don't confuse scaling up (vertical, a bigger VM) with scaling out (horizontal, more VMs) — the exam tests this distinction directly, and it comes up again in the Azure Compute module.
CapEx vs. OpEx questions are usually straightforward if you remember: CapEx means buying hardware upfront; OpEx means paying only for what you actually use, as you use it.

commonMistakes.mistake: "IaaS means Microsoft manages everything."
commonMistakes.correction: In IaaS, Microsoft only manages the physical infrastructure and virtualization layer — you still manage the operating system, runtime, and applications yourself.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Hybrid cloud just means using two different cloud providers."
commonMistakes.correction: That's multi-cloud. Hybrid cloud specifically means combining on-premises or private infrastructure with public cloud services.

commonMistakes.mistake: "Elasticity and scalability are the same thing."
commonMistakes.correction: Scalability is the ability to increase or decrease resources, often through planned or manual action. Elasticity is the automatic, on-demand adjustment of resources to match real-time demand.

commonMistakes.mistake: "In SaaS, the customer has no responsibilities at all."
commonMistakes.correction: Even in SaaS, the customer is still responsible for their data, devices, and accounts and identities — Microsoft never takes over that part, regardless of service model.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the shared responsibility model, which of the following is the customer always responsible for, in every service model?
options: Physical servers
Their data and identities
The hypervisor
Networking hardware
knowledgeCheck.explanation: No matter which service model you use — IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS — you always retain responsibility for your own data and for managing identities and access. Physical infrastructure, the hypervisor, and networking hardware are increasingly managed by Microsoft as you move toward SaaS.

knowledgeCheck.question: A company automatically adds more web server instances during a flash sale, then removes them afterward without any manual action. Which concept does this describe?
options: Elasticity
Scalability
High availability
Fault tolerance
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Elasticity specifically means resources automatically scale up or down to match real-time demand, with no manual intervention required. Scalability is the broader ability to add or remove capacity, which can be manual or automatic.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which cloud deployment model combines on-premises infrastructure with public cloud services?
options: Multi-cloud
Private cloud
Hybrid cloud
Community cloud
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises or private infrastructure with public cloud services, often chosen for compliance, data residency, or legacy-system reasons. Multi-cloud instead means using two or more public cloud providers together.

azure-architecture.title: Azure Architecture

sections.heading: Azure's Physical Foundation: Regions and Zones
sections.body: Every Azure resource you create ultimately runs on physical hardware sitting in a real datacenter somewhere in the world, and understanding how Microsoft organizes that hardware geographically helps explain many of the choices you'll make when designing a solution. Azure groups its datacenters into regions, and within many regions those datacenters are further split into availability zones - physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling, and networking, so that a fire, flood, or power outage in one zone doesn't take down the others. Regions themselves are matched with a partner elsewhere in the world to form a region pair, giving Microsoft a coordinated way to roll out platform updates and recover services if an entire region were ever lost. Zooming out further, groups of regions across a broad area make up a geography, which matters most for organizations that need to guarantee customer data stays within a particular legal or regulatory boundary, such as a country or continent. None of this physical layout is something you manage day to day, but every time you pick a region for a new resource, you're implicitly choosing which of these physical protections apply to it.

sections.heading: Containers for Your Resources: Resource Groups and Subscriptions
sections.body: Once you know where a resource will physically live, you need somewhere logical to put it, and that's where resource groups come in. Think of a resource group as a folder that holds everything related to one solution - a web app, its database, its storage account, and its networking components can all sit inside a single resource group so you can see, manage, and eventually retire them as a unit. That last part matters more than it might seem: deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it, so a resource group is a lifecycle boundary as much as an organizational one, not just a label. Above resource groups sits the subscription, which acts as the billing and access boundary for everything underneath it; a subscription ties usage back to a payment method and an Azure Active Directory tenant, and it's the level at which many cost management and access controls are first configured. A single organization might run one subscription for everything, or split workloads across several subscriptions - for example, separating development from production, or isolating one department's spending from another's.

sections.heading: The Full Governance Hierarchy and How Inheritance Works
sections.body: Resource groups and subscriptions don't exist in isolation - they sit inside a larger structure that Azure uses to apply governance consistently across an entire organization. At the top sits the management group, a container that can hold multiple subscriptions (or even other management groups), letting a large company apply one set of rules across every subscription it owns instead of configuring each one separately. Below the management group comes the subscription, below that the resource group, and below that the individual resource itself - a VM, a storage account, a database, or whatever else you've deployed. What makes this hierarchy powerful in practice is inheritance: an Azure Policy or a role-based access control (RBAC) assignment applied at any level automatically applies to everything nested beneath it, unless something more specific further down explicitly overrides it. Assign a policy that blocks a certain region at the management group level, and every subscription, resource group, and resource under it inherits that restriction immediately, with no need to reapply it four different times. This is the mechanism that lets a small governance team manage security and compliance for a company with hundreds of subscriptions without touching each one individually.

sections.heading: Deploying Consistently with Resource Manager and ARM Templates
sections.body: Every action you take in Azure - clicking Create in the portal, running a CLI command, calling PowerShell, or hitting the REST API directly - ends up going through the same underlying service: Azure Resource Manager, or ARM. ARM is the layer that receives the request, checks who's asking and whether they're authorized, and then creates, updates, or deletes the resource accordingly, which is also why RBAC and policy enforcement work consistently no matter which tool someone used to make the request. Rather than clicking through the portal by hand every time you need to stand up the same environment, you can describe your desired infrastructure once in an ARM template - a JSON file listing the resources, their settings, and how they relate to each other - and hand that file to Resource Manager to deploy. Because the template is declarative, meaning it describes the end state you want rather than a sequence of steps to get there, you can run the same template against an empty subscription or one that already partially matches it, and Resource Manager will figure out what needs to be created or changed to match the template. This is what people mean by infrastructure as code: your environment's definition lives in a file you can review, version, and reuse, instead of in someone's memory of which buttons they clicked.

sections.heading: Designing for Resilience: Availability Sets vs. Availability Zones
sections.body: Regions and zones describe where Microsoft's datacenters physically sit, but you still have to decide how to arrange your own virtual machines within that layout to avoid downtime. An availability set is a logical grouping you assign VMs to within a single datacenter so that Azure spreads them across separate fault domains, which share power and network hardware, and update domains, which are patched and rebooted at different times, meaning a hardware fault or planned maintenance won't take out every VM in your set simultaneously. Availability zones solve a bigger version of the same problem: instead of protecting you within one datacenter, they let you spread VMs across two or more physically separate datacenters within the same region, each with independent power and cooling, so that the loss of an entire facility still leaves your application running elsewhere. In practice, you choose based on the scale of failure you're protecting against and what the region supports - availability zones give stronger protection when they're available, while availability sets remain useful for resilience within a single datacenter or in regions where zones aren't offered.

keyTakeaways: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the single control plane behind every deployment method - portal, CLI, PowerShell, and SDKs all route through it.
ARM templates describe the desired end state of your infrastructure in JSON, so deployments become repeatable, version-controllable, and consistent across environments.
Policies and role assignments made at a management group or subscription flow downward automatically to every resource group and resource nested beneath them.
Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it in one action, which makes it efficient for cleanup but risky if used carelessly.
Regions are built from one or more datacenters, and many are subdivided into availability zones so a single facility failure doesn't take down an entire region.
Region pairs and geographies exist above individual regions to support coordinated disaster recovery and to satisfy data residency and compliance requirements.
examTips: When a question describes wanting to apply one setting (a policy, a budget, or an RBAC role) to many subscriptions at once, the answer is almost always management group, not subscription or resource group.

If a scenario mentions repeatable, consistent, or automated deployment of the same infrastructure to multiple environments, look for ARM template or infrastructure as code in the answer choices rather than manual portal steps.
Watch for questions that test the consequence of deletion - AZ-900 likes to ask what happens to resources when their parent resource group is removed, and the answer is that they are deleted too.
Memorize the hierarchy order cold: management group sits above subscription, which sits above resource group, which sits above the individual resource - reordering it is a common wrong-answer trap.
Questions about resilience often hinge on scale of failure: a single-datacenter hardware or maintenance event points to availability sets, while a datacenter-wide outage points to availability zones.

commonMistakes.mistake: I think a resource group is just a folder for organizing resources visually, so it doesn't really matter what I put in one together.
commonMistakes.correction: A resource group is also a management and lifecycle boundary - resources in it can be deployed, managed, and deleted together, and deleting the group deletes everything inside it, so grouping choices have real operational consequences.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed ARM templates only work for creating brand-new resources.
commonMistakes.correction: ARM templates are declarative - you can run the same template against an environment that already has some or all of those resources, and Resource Manager will update whatever doesn't already match the desired state, which is why deployments are described as idempotent.

commonMistakes.mistake: I figured permissions and policies have to be set individually on every subscription or resource group to make sure they're applied everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: Assigning a policy or role at a management group, or any higher scope, automatically applies it to everything nested beneath it - that inheritance is the whole point of the hierarchy, letting you set a rule once at the right level instead of repeating it everywhere.

commonMistakes.mistake: I think a subscription is the top of the Azure hierarchy, so there's nothing above it to worry about.
commonMistakes.correction: Management groups sit above subscriptions and let an organization apply governance across many subscriptions at once; a subscription is only the top of the hierarchy if no management group has been created above it.

knowledgeCheck.question: A company applies an Azure Policy at the management group level to block resource creation in a specific region. What happens to the subscriptions and resource groups nested beneath that management group?
options: The policy automatically applies to all of them unless a lower-level assignment overrides it
The policy only applies to the management group itself, not anything beneath it
Each subscription must have the policy manually reapplied
The policy applies only to resource groups, skipping subscriptions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Azure's hierarchy is designed so that governance controls like policies and RBAC roles assigned at a higher scope automatically flow down to every subscription, resource group, and resource nested within it, unless something more specific overrides them.

knowledgeCheck.question: In what format are Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates written?
options: JSON
XML
YAML
Compiled binary
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ARM templates are JSON files that declaratively describe the resources you want deployed and their configuration; Resource Manager reads the file and creates or updates resources to match it.

knowledgeCheck.question: If you delete a resource group in Azure, what happens to the resources it contains?
options: They are permanently deleted along with the resource group
They are automatically moved to a new default resource group
They remain running but become inaccessible
They are archived for 30 days before deletion
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Deleting a resource group deletes every resource inside it, which is why resource groups are a convenient way to clean up an entire project or environment in one action, but also why care must be taken before deleting one.

azure-compute.title: Azure Compute

sections.heading: What Is 'Compute,' and Why Does Azure Offer So Many Options?
sections.body: In cloud terminology, 'compute' simply means the raw processing power that runs your applications and code, the CPU, memory, and execution environment your workload actually runs on. Every app, whether it's a website, a mobile backend, or a batch job, needs somewhere to execute, and Azure offers a whole family of compute services rather than a single one-size-fits-all option. The reason for this variety is that different workloads have wildly different needs. Some teams want full control over the operating system and everything installed on it. Others just want to upload their code and never think about servers again. Azure's compute portfolio exists to let you pick a point along a spectrum: at one end you manage almost everything yourself and get maximum flexibility, and at the other end Azure manages almost everything and you get maximum convenience. Understanding this spectrum, and where each major compute service sits on it, is the single most useful mental model for this entire domain.

sections.heading: Azure Virtual Machines: The IaaS Foundation
sections.body: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) are the most fundamental compute building block and the clearest example of Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). When you create a VM, Azure hands you a virtual computer, complete with virtual CPU, memory, disks, and networking, running on Azure's physical hardware. From there, you choose the operating system, install whatever software your application needs, configure it however you like, and manage it much like you would a physical server sitting in your own data center. This gives you enormous flexibility: if a workload needs a specific OS version, a particular driver, or unusual software combinations that wouldn't fit a managed platform, a VM can almost always accommodate it. The tradeoff is that flexibility comes with responsibility. You are the one who has to keep the OS updated, secure the machine, and manage its configuration over time, because Azure's job ends at the virtualization layer and the physical hardware underneath it. VMs are the right starting point for understanding compute precisely because every other service in this lesson can be thought of as 'taking away' some of that manual work in exchange for less control.

sections.heading: App Service: Platform as a Service for Web Workloads
sections.body: Azure App Service moves a step further along the spectrum into Platform as a Service (PaaS). Instead of giving you a virtual machine you have to configure, App Service gives you a ready-made hosting environment specifically designed for web applications, REST APIs, and mobile backends. You bring your application code (in languages like .NET, Java, Node.js, Python, or PHP) and App Service takes care of provisioning the underlying servers, installing and patching the operating system, configuring the web server, and keeping the runtime up to date. This is the essence of PaaS: Azure manages the platform your code runs on, while you focus on the application itself. That doesn't mean you have zero responsibilities, you still own your application code, its dependencies, its configuration settings, and its data, but the operational burden of keeping servers healthy and patched disappears from your task list. For teams that want to ship web applications quickly without hiring dedicated infrastructure staff, App Service removes an entire category of day-to-day maintenance work.

sections.heading: Containers: Packaging Applications for Portability
sections.body: Containers sit conceptually between VMs and fully managed platforms, and they solve a different problem than either one: consistency. A container packages an application together with everything it needs to run, its code, libraries, and configuration, into a single lightweight unit that behaves the same way no matter where it's deployed. Unlike a virtual machine, a container doesn't include a full copy of the operating system; instead, it shares the host machine's OS kernel, which makes containers much smaller and faster to start than VMs. This matters because it lets developers build an application once and trust that it will run identically on a laptop, in testing, and in production, eliminating the classic 'it worked on my machine' problem. Azure offers more than one way to run containers, reflecting the same control-versus-convenience spectrum seen elsewhere in compute: some options hand you more orchestration control, while others let you simply run a container without thinking about the machines underneath it at all. The key conceptual point to hold onto is that a container is a portable, self-contained packaging format, not a smaller virtual machine.

sections.heading: Serverless Computing and Azure Functions
sections.body: At the far end of the spectrum from Virtual Machines sits serverless computing, and Azure Functions is its flagship example. The name 'serverless' is a bit misleading, since servers obviously still exist somewhere, but the point is that you never provision, see, or manage them. You simply write a piece of code that responds to a trigger, such as an HTTP request, a message arriving in a queue, or a file being uploaded, and Azure handles everything else: allocating compute resources the instant the trigger fires, scaling that capacity up or down automatically based on demand, and releasing it entirely when there's nothing to do. This has a direct financial consequence that's central to the serverless value proposition: you're typically billed for the actual execution time your code consumes, down to fractions of a second, rather than for reserved capacity sitting idle. Serverless computing is ideal for workloads that are triggered intermittently or unpredictably, where paying for an always-on server would be wasteful.

sections.heading: Choosing Between IaaS, Containers, PaaS, and Serverless
sections.body: With four broad categories on the table, the decision of which to use comes down to one recurring question: how much control do you need, and how much operational work are you willing to take on to get it? If your workload demands a specific OS configuration, legacy software, or fine-grained control over networking and security at the machine level, Virtual Machines and IaaS give you that, at the cost of ongoing maintenance. If you want portability and consistency across environments without owning full servers, containers are a strong middle ground. If you're building a standard web application or API and would rather never think about the underlying server, App Service and PaaS let you hand that off while still owning your code and configuration. And if your workload is genuinely event-driven, sporadic, or you want to pay only for the moments your code actually executes, serverless computing with Azure Functions removes infrastructure concerns almost entirely. None of these options is objectively 'best'; the right choice depends entirely on matching the workload's requirements to how much of the underlying platform you actually need to touch.

keyTakeaways: Azure compute forms a spectrum from Virtual Machines (IaaS) through containers to App Service (PaaS) to Azure Functions (serverless), with control decreasing and convenience increasing along that path.
Virtual Machines give you full control over the operating system and installed software, but you are responsible for maintaining and patching them yourself.
App Service is a PaaS specifically built for hosting web apps and APIs, letting you focus on code while Azure manages the underlying platform.
A container packages an application with its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit that shares the host operating system's kernel rather than including its own full OS.
Serverless computing, exemplified by Azure Functions, runs your code in response to triggers and typically bills you only for the actual execution time consumed.
Moving from IaaS toward serverless always trades away some customer control in exchange for Azure taking on more operational responsibility.
Choosing a compute service is a business tradeoff between operational control and management convenience, not a matter of one option being universally superior.
examTips: AZ-900 scenario questions often describe a business need in plain language, such as 'wants to run code only when triggered, without managing any servers,' and expect you to map that description to the right category, so practice translating scenarios into IaaS, container, PaaS, or serverless without the product name being given away.

Watch for characteristic keyword traps: phrases like 'full control over the operating system' point to VMs/IaaS, 'focus only on application code' points to PaaS or serverless, and 'pay only when the code runs' points specifically to serverless.

Questions are sometimes framed as ranking or comparison questions, such as asking which option requires the least infrastructure management, rather than asking you to define a single service in isolation, so be comfortable placing all four categories along the same spectrum.

If a question emphasizes packaging an app consistently across environments rather than orchestration or scaling, it is testing the basic concept of a container, not a specific container service, so don't overcomplicate it.
Don't assume 'newest' or 'most modern' equals 'most control'; serverless is the newest-feeling option but deliberately offers the least control, while VMs remain the most control-heavy choice.

commonMistakes.mistake: I figure that with PaaS like App Service, Azure manages literally everything, so I have basically no responsibilities at all.
commonMistakes.correction: With PaaS you still own your application code, its dependencies, its configuration, and your data; Azure only takes over the underlying OS, runtime, and infrastructure management, not your application itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Serverless means there are no servers involved anywhere in the picture.
commonMistakes.correction: Servers still run your code behind the scenes; 'serverless' means you never provision or manage them yourself, and you're billed based on actual execution time rather than for reserved server capacity.

commonMistakes.mistake: A container is basically just a smaller, faster virtual machine.
commonMistakes.correction: A container is a fundamentally different packaging model: it bundles an app with its dependencies and shares the host machine's OS kernel, whereas a VM includes and runs its own separate full operating system.

commonMistakes.mistake: IaaS must be the cheapest option since I'm closest to the raw hardware and not paying for a managed platform.
commonMistakes.correction: IaaS often costs more in total once you factor in the time and staff needed to patch, secure, and maintain the VM yourself; PaaS or serverless can end up cheaper overall for workloads that don't need that level of control.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants to run application code without ever provisioning or managing any servers, and wants to be billed based on how much the code actually executes rather than for reserved capacity. Which characteristic best describes the compute model they're describing?
options: Serverless computing, where you're billed for actual execution time and never manage the underlying servers
IaaS, where you provision a virtual machine and are billed for the reserved server capacity
A dedicated on-premises server that you purchase and operate yourself
A colocation arrangement where you own hardware housed in someone else's data center
knowledgeCheck.explanation: This describes serverless computing: Azure allocates resources only when your code runs and bills you for that execution time, with no server provisioning or management required on your part.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which statement best describes what a container is, as distinct from a virtual machine?
options: A lightweight package containing an application and its dependencies that shares the host machine's operating system kernel
A virtual machine that has been resized to use fewer CPU cores and less memory
A dedicated physical server reserved exclusively for a single customer's workload
A billing construct that charges only for the exact seconds your application code executes
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A container bundles an application with its dependencies and shares the host OS kernel rather than including a full separate operating system, which is what makes it lighter weight and faster to start than a virtual machine.

knowledgeCheck.question: A developer is deciding between hosting a standard web API on App Service versus building it on a Virtual Machine. What is the main tradeoff they are weighing?
options: App Service reduces how much infrastructure they must manage themselves, while a VM gives them more direct control over the OS at the cost of ongoing maintenance
There is no real tradeoff, since App Service and Virtual Machines provide identical levels of control and management responsibility
A Virtual Machine is only usable for background batch jobs and cannot host a web API at all
App Service requires the developer to personally patch and secure the operating system, unlike a Virtual Machine
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The core tradeoff along the compute spectrum is control versus convenience: App Service (PaaS) hands off OS and runtime management to Azure, while a VM (IaaS) keeps that control, and that responsibility, with the developer.

azure-networking.title: Azure Networking

sections.heading: What Is a Virtual Network, Really?
sections.body: Every resource you deploy in Azure — a VM, a database, an app service — needs a way to send and receive traffic, and that starts with a Virtual Network, or VNet. Think of a VNet as your own private, isolated slice of network space carved out inside Azure's datacenters. When you create one, you assign it a range of IP addresses (an address space, such as 10.0.0.0/16) that belongs entirely to you. Nothing outside that VNet can see or reach the resources inside it unless you deliberately open a path, and nothing inside automatically talks to the outside world in ways you haven't configured. This is the foundation everything else in this lesson builds on: subnets divide a VNet up, security rules control what crosses its boundaries, and gateways and peering connect it to other networks. A VNet by itself isn't a physical piece of hardware — it is a logical construct, but it behaves exactly like a traditional network you might build in an on-premises datacenter, just software-defined and elastic.

sections.heading: Subnets: Carving Up the Neighborhood
sections.body: A single VNet can hold a lot of resources, and lumping everything together makes it hard to organize or secure sensibly. That is where subnets come in: a subnet is simply a smaller range of addresses carved out of the VNet's overall address space, used to group related resources together. A common pattern is to put front-end web servers in one subnet and back-end database servers in another, so that each group can be managed, secured, and monitored on its own terms — for example, only the web subnet needs to accept traffic from the internet, while the database subnet should never be directly reachable from outside. Importantly, subnets within the same VNet are not isolated from each other by default: Azure automatically creates system routes that let resources in different subnets of the same VNet reach one another over the Microsoft network, with no extra gateway or peering required. Segmentation into subnets is therefore primarily an organizational and security tool, not a way to block traffic on its own — that job belongs to the next piece.

sections.heading: Network Security Groups: Controlling Who Gets Through
sections.body: If subnets are how you organize your resources, a Network Security Group (NSG) is how you decide who is allowed to talk to them. An NSG is a set of rules you attach to a subnet or to an individual network interface, and each rule describes a piece of traffic by its source, destination, port, and protocol, then says whether to allow or deny it. The important mechanical detail worth remembering is that every rule has a priority number, and Azure evaluates rules in order from lowest number to highest — as soon as traffic matches a rule, that rule's action is applied and no further rules are checked, even if a later rule might also have matched. NSGs also come with a small set of built-in default rules (for instance, allowing traffic within the VNet and allowing outbound internet access) that apply unless you override them with rules of your own. Because an NSG works purely on addresses, ports, and protocols, it cannot look inside the traffic to understand what application-level request is being made — for that kind of deeper inspection, you need a dedicated firewall service.

sections.heading: Connecting Networks: Peering, VPN Gateway, and ExpressRoute
sections.body: Sooner or later, a single VNet is not enough — you need two VNets to talk to each other, or you need your Azure network to talk to your company's on-premises office or datacenter. Azure gives you a few distinct tools for this, and picking the right one is largely a matter of scope and requirements. When you need to join two VNets together, VNet peering is typically the simplest and fastest choice, since it links them directly over Microsoft's own backbone network rather than routing traffic out to the public internet. When you need to connect an Azure VNet back to an on-premises network, you generally reach for a VPN Gateway, which encrypts traffic and sends it over the public internet in a protected tunnel — a good fit when cost matters more than guaranteed bandwidth or latency. When an organization needs a private, dedicated, high-bandwidth link to Azure that bypasses the public internet entirely — often for compliance reasons or to support very large, latency-sensitive workloads — that is the scenario ExpressRoute exists for. None of these three tools compete with each other so much as answer different versions of the same underlying question: how much distance, cost, and internet exposure am I willing to accept to link these networks together?

sections.heading: Getting Traffic to the Right Place
sections.body: Once your network is built and secured, you still need a way to spread incoming requests across multiple resources so no single VM or server gets overwhelmed, and Azure offers a small family of services for this that are easy to mix up because they all describe themselves as distributing traffic. Azure Load Balancer works at the transport layer — it looks only at IP addresses and ports, forwarding TCP or UDP connections to a pool of backend VMs without understanding anything about the content of the request, which makes it extremely fast but somewhat blunt. Application Gateway operates a layer higher, at the HTTP/HTTPS level, so it can read the actual web request and make smarter routing decisions — for example, sending traffic for /images to one set of servers and /api to another, all within a single region. Azure Front Door takes that same layer-7 awareness and applies it globally, routing users to whichever regional deployment of your application is closest or healthiest, which is what you reach for when your application runs in multiple regions around the world and you want a single global entry point. The pattern to hold onto is: Load Balancer is regional and layer 4, Application Gateway is regional and layer 7, and Front Door is global and layer 7.

sections.heading: Guarding the Perimeter and Speeding Up Delivery
sections.body: NSGs handle basic traffic filtering per subnet or network interface, but larger environments often need centralized, more sophisticated perimeter protection, which is the role Azure Firewall plays. It is a fully managed firewall service that sits in front of your VNets and can filter traffic using richer criteria than an NSG offers, including specific domain names (FQDN filtering) and threat intelligence feeds, all managed as a single consistent policy across many VNets and subscriptions rather than rule-by-rule on each subnet. On the opposite side of the traffic equation — not protecting your network from the world, but making your content reach the world faster — sits Azure CDN, a Content Delivery Network that caches copies of static content like images, videos, and scripts on servers physically distributed around the globe, so users download that content from a nearby location instead of round-tripping all the way back to your original server. Firewall and CDN solve unrelated problems, but both exist for the same underlying reason: as your audience and your infrastructure grow past a single subnet in a single region, you need dedicated services to manage security and performance at scale rather than relying on the basics alone.

keyTakeaways: A VNet is a private, isolated address space in Azure, and nothing crosses its boundary unless you configure a path for it.

Subnets subdivide a VNet's address range so you can group and manage resources separately, but resources in different subnets of the same VNet can reach each other by default through Azure's system routes.
NSG rules are evaluated strictly in priority order — lowest number first — and the first matching rule wins, so later rules are never consulted once a match occurs.

VNet peering connects two VNets over Microsoft's backbone, VPN Gateway connects networks over the encrypted public internet, and ExpressRoute connects networks over a private dedicated line — the right choice depends on scope, cost, and how much internet exposure is acceptable.
Load Balancer works at layer 4 within a region, Application Gateway works at layer 7 within a region, and Front Door works at layer 7 across regions globally.
Azure Firewall provides centralized, policy-based filtering with capabilities like FQDN filtering that go beyond what an NSG's simple allow/deny rules can do.
CDN caches static content close to users to speed up delivery, which is a different job from routing decisions handled by Load Balancer, Application Gateway, or Front Door.
examTips: When a scenario asks how to connect two VNets in the same region as cheaply and simply as possible, the expected answer is usually VNet peering, not a gateway.

Look for OSI-layer language as a shortcut: 'Layer 4' or 'transport' points to Load Balancer, while 'Layer 7', 'HTTP', or 'URL-based routing' points to Application Gateway; 'global' or 'multiple regions' points to Front Door.
If a question mentions filtering by domain name (FQDN) or applying one security policy across many VNets, that is describing Azure Firewall, not an NSG — NSGs only match on IP, port, and protocol.

Do not assume CDN and Front Door are interchangeable on the exam — CDN questions tend to emphasize caching static content near users, while Front Door questions emphasize global HTTP routing and failover between regions.
When a question describes needing a connection that never touches the public internet for compliance or heavy bandwidth reasons, that is the signal for ExpressRoute rather than VPN Gateway.

commonMistakes.mistake: I need to configure something before two VMs in the same subnet can talk to each other.
commonMistakes.correction: Resources within the same subnet can already communicate by default. NSGs and other rules only come into play when you explicitly need to allow or block specific traffic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Two subnets in the same VNet can't reach each other unless I set up peering or a gateway.
commonMistakes.correction: Peering and gateways are for connecting separate VNets or external networks. Subnets inside a single VNet are automatically routable to one another through Azure's default system routes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Application Gateway and Load Balancer are really the same product with two different names.
commonMistakes.correction: Load Balancer distributes TCP/UDP traffic at layer 4 without inspecting content, while Application Gateway understands HTTP/HTTPS requests at layer 7 and can route based on things like URL path — they solve related but distinct problems.

commonMistakes.mistake: As long as traffic passes my NSG, the resources behind it are fully protected.
commonMistakes.correction: An NSG is one layer of defense based on simple address/port/protocol rules. Sensitive environments typically add Azure Firewall for deeper filtering and other controls like private endpoints as part of a layered security approach.

knowledgeCheck.question: A company wants to manage its web servers and database servers with different security rules, but keep both groups within a single Azure network so they can communicate easily. What should they create inside their VNet to achieve this?
options: Two separate VNets connected by peering
Two subnets within the same VNet
Two NSGs with no subnets defined
Two separate resource groups
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Subnets let you divide a VNet's address space into groups so different sets of resources can be organized and secured separately, while still allowing communication within the same VNet by default.

knowledgeCheck.question: A VNet contains Subnet A and Subnet B, with no peering, gateway, or custom routes configured between them. Can a VM in Subnet A reach a VM in Subnet B?
options: No, subnets are isolated from each other by default
Yes, Azure automatically routes traffic between subnets in the same VNet
Only if ExpressRoute is configured
Only if both subnets have identical NSG rules
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Azure creates default system routes that allow resources in different subnets within the same VNet to communicate automatically, without requiring peering, a gateway, or ExpressRoute.

knowledgeCheck.question: An NSG has multiple rules that could match the same piece of traffic. How does Azure determine which rule is actually applied?
options: The rule with the lowest priority number is evaluated first, and the first match wins
All matching rules are applied together
The most recently created rule always wins
Rules are applied in alphabetical order by name
knowledgeCheck.explanation: NSG rules are processed in order of priority number, from lowest to highest, and processing stops as soon as a rule matches — later rules are not evaluated once a match is found.

azure-storage.title: Azure Storage

sections.heading: The Azure Storage Account: One Front Door, Many Services
sections.body: Every piece of data you put in Azure Storage lives inside a storage account — think of it as the single container, billing boundary, and namespace that groups together whichever storage services you decide to use. When you create a storage account, you're not committing to just one type of data; the same account can simultaneously hold blob containers, file shares, queues, and tables, each reachable through its own unique URL under that account's name. This matters because real applications rarely need only one shape of data: a web app might store user-uploaded photos as blobs, keep session state in a queue, and log click events in a table, all from the same account. Understanding that the storage account is the umbrella — and that the specific service, access tier, and redundancy setting are choices you layer on top of it — is the foundation for everything else in this lesson.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Storage Service: Blobs, Files, Queues, and Tables
sections.body: Azure gives you four core storage services, and picking the right one comes down to a simple question: what shape does your data take, and how will something read it back? Blob Storage is built for data that doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns — photos, video files, log dumps, backups, or any binary object you just need to store and retrieve by name; it scales to enormous size and is what most people picture when they think 'cloud storage.' Azure Files takes a different approach: instead of accessing data through an API or SDK, you mount it as a shared network drive using the same SMB or NFS protocols your on-premises file servers already speak, which makes it the natural choice when you're migrating legacy applications that expect a normal file path rather than a web request. Queue Storage exists to solve a very specific coordination problem: when one part of an application produces work faster than another part can consume it, a queue lets messages pile up safely in between, so components can operate independently without losing work or crashing under load. Table Storage, meanwhile, is a simple NoSQL store for key-value style data — rows of information you look up quickly by key, without the overhead of a relational database schema, which suits things like device metadata or user preferences where the data is simple and access patterns are predictable. None of these services compete with each other so much as divide the labor: a single application often uses two or three of them side by side.

sections.heading: Access Tiers: Balancing Cost Against How Often You Need Your Data
sections.body: Not all data is read equally often, and Azure lets you pay accordingly through access tiers, which apply at the blob level. The Hot tier is tuned for data you expect to touch frequently — it costs more to store but the least to read, which makes sense for anything actively in use, like the images behind a live website. The Cool tier flips that balance: storage is cheaper, but reading the data back costs more, so it fits information you need to keep around but don't expect to open often, such as a monthly backup you hope you never have to restore. Archive pushes the tradeoff to its extreme — the cheapest possible storage cost, but data isn't instantly available; retrieving an archived blob requires a rehydration step that can take hours before the file is usable again, so it's meant for data kept purely for retention or compliance rather than anything you might need on short notice. The skill being tested here isn't memorizing three names, it's recognizing that the 'right' tier is a function of how predictably and how soon you'll need the data back, and that moving data to a colder tier is a bet that you won't need fast access before you need cheap storage.

sections.heading: Redundancy: How Azure Keeps Your Data Alive
sections.body: Storing data in only one place is a risk, so Azure Storage always keeps multiple copies of your data — the redundancy option you choose just determines how many copies exist and how far apart they are. Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three copies within a single datacenter, protecting you against ordinary hardware failure but not against an event that takes out the whole building. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) spreads those three copies across separate availability zones within the same region — physically distinct facilities with their own power and networking — so a zone-level outage doesn't take your data with it. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) takes the LRS model and adds a second, geographically distant paired region, asynchronously copying your data there so it survives even a regional disaster. Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) combines both ideas: zone-level protection in the primary region plus a replicated copy in a secondary region, giving you the highest level of durability Azure offers for a single storage account. Reading this progression is the real exam skill: each step up adds a specific kind of protection, so you should be able to work backward from a stated risk — 'what if a whole datacenter fails' versus 'what if a whole region fails' — to the redundancy option that actually addresses it, rather than assuming more copies is always the answer.

sections.heading: Keeping Data Organized, Secure, and Compliant
sections.body: Beyond deciding where and how many copies of your data live, Azure gives you tools to manage it responsibly over time. Lifecycle management policies let you define rules — based on how old a blob is or when it was last accessed — that automatically move data between tiers or delete it outright, so a rule might shift blobs from Hot to Cool after 30 days and into Archive after a year, all without anyone manually babysitting storage costs. When you need to grant someone temporary, limited access to your storage — a mobile app uploading a photo, or a partner downloading a single file — a shared access signature (SAS) is the tool for the job: it's a signed URL that grants specific permissions, such as read-only or write-only, to specific resources for a specific window of time, without ever handing over the account's full keys. For data that must not change once it's written — financial records, legal documents, audit logs — immutable storage locks blobs into a write-once-read-many (WORM) state for a retention period you define, during which the data genuinely cannot be modified or deleted by anyone, including an administrator, which is often the exact guarantee a regulator is asking for. Together, these tools mean you're not just choosing where data lives, but actively managing its cost, its accessibility, and its integrity throughout its lifetime.

keyTakeaways: A single Azure Storage account can host Blob, File, Queue, and Table storage together under one billing and management boundary.
Blob Storage holds unstructured data, Azure Files provides a mountable network share, Queue Storage decouples application components, and Table Storage offers simple key-value lookups.
Access tiers trade storage cost against retrieval cost and speed — Hot for frequent access, Cool for infrequent access, Archive for rarely-touched compliance data that can wait hours to be read.
Redundancy options multiply the number and location of data copies, from 3 copies in one datacenter (LRS) up to 6 copies spanning zones and a paired region (GZRS).

Choosing a colder tier or higher redundancy is a deliberate tradeoff, not automatically 'better' — it should match actual recovery and access requirements, not just chase the biggest number of copies.
Lifecycle management policies automate moving or deleting blobs based on age or last-access rules, removing the need for manual tier management.
Shared access signatures grant narrow, time-limited permissions instead of full account credentials, and immutable (WORM) storage prevents changes or deletion for a defined retention period.
examTips: The exam frequently poses scenarios rather than definitions — instead of asking 'what is LRS,' it describes a business need ('must survive loss of an entire datacenter but budget is tight') and expects you to map it to the right redundancy option.

Watch for tier questions that hide the real constraint in a single word: 'rarely,' 'archived,' 'compliance for years,' or 'must be available immediately' are the signals that decide between Cool and Archive.

When a question mixes a storage service with a tier or redundancy option, answer them independently: the service answers 'what kind of data,' while tier and redundancy answer 'how it's accessed and protected' — don't let one distractor blur the other.

Questions about management tools often list AzCopy, Storage Explorer, and CLI/PowerShell together as distractors — know that AzCopy is command-line and scriptable while Storage Explorer is the graphical tool, since the exam likes to swap these labels.

If a scenario says data 'must remain accessible during a full regional outage,' a GRS or GZRS class answer is required; if it only says 'protect against hardware failure,' LRS is often the intended, cheapest correct answer — don't over-engineer toward the fanciest redundancy option.

commonMistakes.mistake: I figured moving blobs to the Archive tier just makes them a little slower to open, like a cache miss.
commonMistakes.correction: Archive isn't just 'slower' — data must be rehydrated back to an online tier first, a process that can take hours, so Archive is only appropriate for data you don't need on short notice, not simply 'cold' data you might grab any minute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Since GZRS protects against both zone and region failures, I assumed it's always the right choice and GRS is basically obsolete.
commonMistakes.correction: GZRS costs more than GRS for the added zone-level protection in the primary region. If a workload doesn't require that extra layer, or the region doesn't support availability zones, GRS remains a valid and cheaper way to meet a cross-region durability requirement.

commonMistakes.mistake: I thought a shared access signature was just another way of logging in with the storage account's username and password.
commonMistakes.correction: A SAS is a time-limited, scoped token that grants specific permissions to specific resources, not a full credential. It expires and can be restricted to read-only or a single container, which is exactly why it's safer to hand out than the account's access keys.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed Azure Files was just Blob Storage with a different name, since both store 'files' in the cloud.
commonMistakes.correction: Azure Files is mounted like a network file share using SMB or NFS, so existing applications can read and write to it with normal file paths, whereas Blob Storage is accessed through APIs and SDKs as objects — the two solve different integration problems even though both can hold file-like data.

knowledgeCheck.question: A finance team must retain seven years of monthly statements for compliance. The files are rarely opened, but if auditors request one, staff need to view it within minutes, not hours. Which access tier best fits this requirement?
options: Archive
Cool
Hot
Premium
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Archive is the cheapest to store but can take hours to rehydrate before a blob is readable, which fails the 'within minutes' requirement. Cool offers low storage cost while still allowing prompt access, making it the better fit for infrequently accessed data that must remain quickly retrievable.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants their storage account's data to survive the loss of an entire Azure region, but they don't need the primary region itself to tolerate a zone-level outage, and they want to keep costs as low as possible while still meeting that regional-failure requirement. Which redundancy option should they choose?
options: LRS
ZRS
GRS
GZRS
knowledgeCheck.explanation: GRS replicates data from the primary region to a second, distant region, satisfying the 'survive a full region loss' requirement without paying for the zone-level protection that GZRS adds in the primary region, making it the lower-cost option that still meets the stated need.

knowledgeCheck.question: An application needs to store blob containers, file shares, and queues, and wants all of them to share the same billing and access boundary. What single Azure resource makes this possible?
options: A storage account
A resource group
A subscription
A management group
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A storage account is the unique namespace that can hold multiple storage services — blobs, files, queues, and tables — together, giving them a shared billing boundary and access point, distinct from broader organizational scopes like resource groups or subscriptions.

identity.title: Identity

sections.heading: Two Different Questions: Who Are You, and What Can You Do?
sections.body: Every time you sign in to a system, that system is quietly working through two separate questions, in a strict order. The first question is: are you really who you claim to be? Answering that question is the job of authentication, and it happens through things like a password, a fingerprint, or a one-time code from your phone. Only once that question is settled does the system move on to the second question: now that we know who you are, what exactly are you permitted to do? That is authorization, and it decides which files you can open, which resources you can create or delete, and which parts of the system stay off-limits to you. It helps to picture a large office building with a security desk. Authentication is the moment the guard checks your ID badge and confirms it belongs to you. Authorization is what happens after that, when your badge is scanned at a specific door and either lets you through or doesn't, depending on which floors you're cleared for. You cannot skip straight to authorization without authentication happening first, because the system has to know who you are before it can look up what you're allowed to touch. Keeping these two stages mentally separate is one of the most useful habits you can build when learning cloud identity, because almost everything else in this module is really just a variation on refining one of these two steps.

sections.heading: Azure Active Directory and the Idea of a Tenant
sections.body: So who actually performs that identity check in Azure? That job belongs to Azure Active Directory, Microsoft's cloud-based service for managing identities and controlling access. Think of it as a directory, in the same sense as a phone directory or an employee directory, except this one holds digital records: user accounts, groups, registered devices, and the applications an organization uses, all in one place. When an organization signs up to use Microsoft cloud services, it doesn't share a directory with every other customer in the world. Instead, it gets its own dedicated, isolated instance of Azure AD, and that dedicated instance is called a tenant. You can think of a tenant as your organization's own private slice of the identity service, walled off from everyone else's, with its own set of users, its own settings, and its own administrators. A single company usually has one tenant that represents the whole organization, and every Azure subscription that company owns is associated with that tenant so that access decisions all trace back to the same trusted set of identities. Understanding the tenant as a boundary is the foundation everything else in this lesson builds on top of.

sections.heading: Proving It's Really You: MFA and Passwordless Sign-In
sections.body: A password by itself has always had a weakness: it's just a string of characters, and strings of characters can be guessed, stolen, or reused across multiple sites without you realizing it. Because of that, modern identity systems lean on the idea of factors, which fall into rough categories: something you know, like a password; something you have, like a phone or a hardware key; and something you are, like a fingerprint. Requiring more than one of these categories together, rather than relying on a password alone, dramatically shrinks the chance that a stolen credential is enough to get someone into your account. Taking this a step further, some sign-in methods remove the password from the equation entirely. With a physical security key or a device-based method like Windows Hello, you prove who you are directly through something you hold or something biometric about you, with no password ever typed or stored to be phished in the first place. These passwordless methods tend to be both more secure, since there's no password to steal, and more convenient, since there's nothing to remember or type. Either way, all of this activity, whether it's a password plus a code, or a fingerprint on its own, still belongs entirely to the authentication stage: it's all about proving identity before any conversation about permissions even begins.

sections.heading: Signing In Once and Reaching Everything: How SSO Fits In
sections.body: Once an organization has dozens or hundreds of cloud and web applications, asking a user to authenticate separately, with a separate password, for every single one becomes exhausting and, ironically, less secure, since people cope with too many passwords by reusing weak ones. Single sign-on solves this by letting a user go through the authentication process once, with a trusted identity provider, and then carry that proof of identity across many connected applications without signing in again for each one. In an Azure environment, the identity provider doing this work is Azure AD itself: it authenticates the user a single time and then issues a token that the user's session presents to any application that trusts that same directory. Each of those applications doesn't need to re-check the password; it just needs to trust the token that Azure AD already vouched for. From the user's perspective, this feels like effortlessly moving between applications; from an organization's perspective, it means fewer passwords to manage, fewer help desk calls about forgotten credentials, and one central place to enforce sign-in rules rather than dozens of separate, inconsistent ones.

sections.heading: Conditional Access: Making the Sign-In Decision Smarter
sections.body: So far, authentication has sounded fairly binary: you prove who you are, and you're either let in or you're not. In practice, Azure AD can be far more nuanced than that through a capability called Conditional Access. Rather than treating every sign-in attempt identically, Conditional Access evaluates the surrounding circumstances of that attempt, such as which user is signing in, what device they're using, where in the world the request is coming from, and how risky that combination looks, and then applies an organization's if-this-then-that policies to decide the outcome. A sign-in from a recognized company laptop on the office network might be waved through with no extra friction, while the exact same username signing in from an unfamiliar country on an unmanaged device might be challenged for an extra verification step, or blocked outright, even though the password entered was completely correct. This turns authentication from a single yes-or-no gate into a continuously evaluated decision that responds to context, which is a core piece of what people mean when they describe identity as the perimeter that really matters in cloud security.

sections.heading: Bringing in the Outside World: B2B and B2C
sections.body: Not everyone who needs to sign in belongs inside your own tenant as a regular employee, and Azure AD offers two different answers depending on who that outside person is. If you need to collaborate with an external partner, vendor, or contractor, giving them access to specific resources without creating and managing a brand-new account for them, you invite them into your tenant as a guest, using the credentials they already have from their own organization; this scenario is what Azure AD External Identities covers for business-to-business collaboration. If, instead, you're building a customer-facing application, like a retail website or a mobile app, where the public at large needs to register and sign in, possibly using a social account they already have, you're dealing with a completely different scale and audience, and that's the scenario built for business-to-customer identity management. The distinction to hold onto is who is on the other end of that sign-in screen: a known partner organization collaborating with you internally, versus the general public consuming something you've built for them externally.

keyTakeaways: Authentication always happens before authorization: you must prove who you are before the system can decide what you're allowed to do.
A tenant is an organization's own dedicated, isolated instance of Azure AD, separate from every other organization's directory.
Multi-factor and passwordless sign-in both strengthen the authentication step, not the authorization step.
Single sign-on lets one successful authentication with Azure AD carry across many trusted applications without repeated logins.
Conditional Access turns sign-in into a context-aware decision, factoring in signals like device, location, and risk rather than a simple yes-or-no gate.
External collaboration with known partner organizations is a business-to-business scenario, while public customer-facing sign-in is a business-to-customer scenario.
Identity checks, MFA prompts, and Conditional Access policies all still belong to the authentication stage; permission checks on resources are what constitute authorization.
examTips: When a question describes a scenario and asks whether it's about authentication or authorization, look for whether the described action is about proving identity (authentication) or about being allowed to perform a specific action or reach a specific resource (authorization) — the exam loves testing this distinction through scenarios rather than definitions.

If a question mentions inviting an external partner organization's users into your tenant, that's a B2B scenario; if it mentions a public-facing website or app letting customers sign up with a social account, that's B2C — watch for these keyword cues rather than assuming they're interchangeable.

Questions describing access decisions that change based on location, device compliance, or risk level are testing Conditional Access, not MFA or SSO on their own — MFA is one possible outcome a Conditional Access policy can require, not the same feature.

When a scenario says a user should only sign in once to reach several different applications, that phrase is a strong signal for SSO, so be ready to pick it over Azure AD or MFA as the more precise answer.

Remember that a tenant is the organizational boundary for identity, which is a different boundary than a subscription (billing and resources) — questions sometimes test whether you can tell these two apart.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking that once MFA is enabled, a user has effectively been both authenticated and authorized in one step.
commonMistakes.correction: MFA only strengthens the authentication step by requiring an extra proof of identity; a separate authorization check still determines what the now-verified user is allowed to access.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a company automatically gets a new tenant every time it creates a new Azure subscription.
commonMistakes.correction: A tenant is the identity boundary for the whole organization, and multiple subscriptions typically belong to and trust the same single tenant rather than each having its own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing SSO means a weaker, shared password is being used across multiple apps.
commonMistakes.correction: SSO means the user authenticates once with a trusted identity provider and receives a token that other trusted applications accept, so no password is being shared or reused across those apps at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating passwordless sign-in as just another name for multi-factor authentication.
commonMistakes.correction: Passwordless authentication removes the password entirely and proves identity through something like a security key or biometric, whereas MFA can still include a password as one of its factors alongside another.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming B2B and B2C are just two names for the same external-user feature.
commonMistakes.correction: B2B is about inviting known partner or vendor users into your own tenant as guests, while B2C is about building and managing identities for the general public in a customer-facing application, which are different audiences and different tools.
