knowledgeCheck.question: In the flow of signing in and reaching a resource, what does Azure AD hand off to the user's session immediately after successfully confirming their identity?
options: A token that other applications and resources can trust
A brand-new user account
A permanent password exemption
A list of every resource in the subscription
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Once Azure AD has verified who a user is, it issues a token representing that proven identity, which is what gets presented onward so resources can perform their own authorization check without re-verifying the password.

knowledgeCheck.question: Two companies merge, and for now each keeps its own separate set of users, groups, and directory settings in Azure AD rather than sharing one. What is each of these separate directory instances best described as?
options: A tenant
A resource group
A management group
A subscription
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A tenant is a dedicated, isolated instance of Azure AD belonging to one organization, so each company keeping its own separate directory of users and settings means each still has its own distinct tenant.

knowledgeCheck.question: A sign-in attempt uses the correct password and passes MFA, but it comes from an unfamiliar country on a device the organization has never seen before, and the request ends up being blocked as a result. Which Azure AD capability is most directly responsible for that context-based decision?
options: Conditional Access
Single sign-on
Azure AD B2C
Passwordless authentication
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Conditional Access evaluates surrounding signals such as location and device before deciding whether to grant, challenge, or block a sign-in, so it is what can override an otherwise correct password and MFA based on context like this.

security.title: Security

sections.heading: Security as a Series of Layers
sections.body: Think about how a museum protects a priceless painting. It doesn't rely on one lock on the front door — there's a fence outside, guards at the entrance, cameras in the halls, a motion-sensor case around the painting, and alarms wired to everything. If a visitor slips past the guards, the case still stops them. Cloud security works the same way. Instead of trying to build one unbeatable wall, Azure wraps a set of independent protective rings around the thing that ultimately matters: your data. Each ring covers a different kind of risk, so a weakness in one doesn't automatically expose everything behind it. Because you don't own or physically visit the buildings your workloads run in, and because your applications are reachable from anywhere on the internet, this layered approach isn't optional decoration — it's how a system with no single walled perimeter can still be trusted with sensitive information.

sections.heading: Physical Security and Identity: The Outermost Layers
sections.body: The very outside of the model is physical security — the concrete, steel, and staffing around Azure's actual datacenters: perimeter fencing, security personnel on site around the clock, biometric checks before anyone reaches a server rack, and surveillance throughout the facility. This is one layer that a customer moving to Azure never has to design, staff, or audit themselves; Microsoft owns it fully regardless of whether you're running virtual machines, containers, or serverless functions. The moment you step inside that boundary, the next layer you actually interact with is identity. Before a network packet is inspected or a firewall rule is checked, the platform has to answer a more basic question: who is asking, and what are they allowed to touch? Every account, every sign-in, and every permission grant lives in this identity layer, which is why getting authentication and access control right is treated as the first real line of defense a customer is responsible for — everything else in the model assumes identity has already done its job correctly.

sections.heading: Perimeter and Network: Controlling the Boundary
sections.body: Moving one ring further in, the perimeter layer is where your environment meets the open internet. This is the boundary where large-scale, blunt-force attacks — like a flood of traffic aimed at knocking a service offline — are absorbed and filtered before they ever reach anything you're running. Once traffic is allowed past that outer edge, the network layer takes over, and its job is different: rather than guarding against the whole internet, it controls how traffic is allowed to move inside your own environment. This is where you divide resources into smaller segments so that a compromise in one part of a network doesn't automatically grant access to every other part, and where administrative access to virtual machines can be routed through a secure, browser-based gateway instead of exposing management ports directly to the internet. Perimeter and network security are often confused because they both sound like 'network stuff,' but the distinction — outer edge versus internal segmentation — shows up regularly in how the model is described.

sections.heading: Compute and Application: Securing What Runs Your Workloads
sections.body: Further in still is the compute layer, which covers the virtual machines, containers, and hosts that actually execute your workloads. Securing this layer means controlling what can run, limiting standing access to management interfaces, and keeping the guest operating system up to date — a responsibility that shifts depending on the service model you choose, since Azure manages the underlying host but you typically manage the software inside an IaaS virtual machine. Sitting just outside the data itself is the application layer, which protects the code, APIs, and logic that users and other systems actually interact with. This is where practices like validating input, filtering malicious web requests before they reach your code, and requiring users to authenticate within the application itself come into play. A vulnerability here — like an application that blindly trusts whatever a user submits — can undermine every layer sitting outside it, which is why application security is treated as its own distinct ring rather than folded into compute.

sections.heading: Data: The Innermost Layer and the Reason for All the Rest
sections.body: At the very center of the model sits data, and everything described so far exists purely to protect it. This is a useful way to reframe the model: it isn't seven equally important boxes sitting side by side — it's six outer rings built specifically to buy the data at the center as much protection as possible before an attacker could ever reach it. At this innermost layer, the questions become very specific to the information itself: who is allowed to read or modify it, how is it classified, and how are the cryptographic keys that protect it managed separately from the data they protect, so that having access to one doesn't automatically mean access to the other. That separation of 'the data' from 'the keys that unlock the data' is a deliberate design choice, and it's the reason a dedicated vault for secrets, keys, and certificates exists as its own service rather than being bundled into storage.

sections.heading: Watching Over It All: Posture, Detection, and Response
sections.body: A model built from seven separate layers is only useful if someone can see across all of them at once, which is why Azure provides tools that sit on top of the whole picture rather than inside any single ring. One gives you a continuously updated, percentage-based read on how closely your configuration matches security best practices, turning a vague sense of 'are we secure?' into a concrete number you can track and improve over time. Another watches for signs that something has actually gone wrong — unusual sign-in patterns, suspicious network activity, malware behavior — and can automatically trigger a response rather than just raising a silent alert. A third service exists specifically to absorb and mitigate the kind of massive, coordinated traffic floods that target the perimeter layer, protecting availability even when the source of the attack is impossible to block one address at a time. None of these tools replace the layers themselves; they exist to give you visibility and control across all of them simultaneously, which is exactly the gap a purely layer-by-layer design would otherwise leave open.

keyTakeaways: Defense in depth arranges independent security layers — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data — so a failure in one layer doesn't expose everything behind it.
Physical security of Azure's datacenters is entirely Microsoft's responsibility, no matter which service model or workload you deploy.
Identity is the first layer a customer is actually responsible for, since every other layer depends on knowing who is making a request.
Perimeter defenses guard the outer edge facing the internet, while network controls govern how traffic moves inside your own environment — these are related but distinct layers.
Compute security includes patching guest operating systems on virtual machines, a responsibility that shifts depending on the service model in use.
Data sits at the center of the model because it's the asset every outer layer exists to protect, not just one peer layer among seven.
Posture, detection, and DDoS mitigation tools operate across the whole layered model rather than living inside any single ring.
examTips: AZ-900 frequently asks 'which layer does this control belong to' — practice mapping specific tools (NSGs, a web application firewall, OS patching, a locked server room) to the correct ring rather than memorizing the ring names alone.

When a question mentions 'multiple layers' or 'no single point of failure' without naming a specific control, the concept being tested is the layered model itself, even if the word for it doesn't appear in the question.

Learn to tell apart tools that sound alike but do different jobs: one gives you a posture score, one detects and responds to active threats, and one absorbs volumetric traffic attacks — questions often hinge on picking the right one for a described scenario.
Watch for shared-responsibility traps embedded in layer questions, such as assuming Microsoft patches a customer-managed VM just because Microsoft also secures the physical datacenter.
If an option describes 'internal segmentation of traffic' versus 'blocking large attacks from the internet,' that's testing network versus perimeter — read carefully before choosing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Defense in depth basically just means having a really strong firewall.
commonMistakes.correction: It means combining multiple independent layers — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data — so that if any one layer is bypassed, the others still stand between an attacker and the data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Since Microsoft secures the datacenter building, Microsoft must also patch the operating system inside my virtual machine.
commonMistakes.correction: Physical security of the facility is entirely Microsoft's job, but keeping the guest operating system patched on an IaaS virtual machine is a customer responsibility.

commonMistakes.mistake: Perimeter security and network security are really just two names for the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: Perimeter security defends the outer boundary facing the internet, while network security controls and segments how traffic moves once it's already inside the environment — they solve different problems.

commonMistakes.mistake: A security posture score is a protection tool that actively blocks attacks.
commonMistakes.correction: A posture score is a measurement — a percentage reflecting how closely your configuration matches security recommendations — not a service that itself intercepts or stops threats.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the defense-in-depth model, which layer sits at the very center and represents the asset that every other layer exists to protect?
options: Network
Application
Data
Perimeter
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Data is placed at the innermost ring of the model. The physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, and application layers all exist to shield this central asset.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following correctly matches a defense-in-depth layer with an example activity that belongs to it?
options: Perimeter — segmenting internal traffic between subnets
Network — absorbing a massive flood of internet traffic
Compute — keeping a virtual machine's guest operating system patched
Application — staffing a datacenter security desk
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Patching the guest OS on a virtual machine is a compute-layer activity. Internal traffic segmentation belongs to the network layer, absorbing internet-wide floods belongs to the perimeter layer, and staffing a datacenter belongs to physical security — not application.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants one tool that continuously monitors their environment for suspicious activity, such as unusual sign-ins or malware behavior, and can respond automatically. Which capability best fits this need?
options: A posture score expressed as a percentage
A cloud-native tool for detecting threats and orchestrating a response
Physical fencing around a datacenter
Segmenting a virtual network into subnets
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Detecting suspicious activity and automatically orchestrating a response describes a threat detection and response capability, distinct from a posture score (which measures configuration, not active threats) and unrelated to physical fencing or subnet segmentation.

governance.title: Governance

sections.heading: Why Governance Exists
sections.body: When a single person spins up a virtual machine for a weekend project, there isn't much need for oversight. But once an organization has dozens of teams, hundreds of subscriptions, and thousands of resources spread across Azure, someone has to answer basic questions at scale: which regions are we allowed to deploy into, who can shut down a production database, and how do we know what a given resource is actually for. Governance is the umbrella term for the tools and processes Azure provides to answer those questions consistently, without a human manually checking every deployment. Rather than relying on one all-powerful control, Azure spreads governance across several complementary mechanisms, each answering a different question: what is allowed, who is allowed to do it, what is protected from change, and how is everything labeled and tracked. Understanding how these pieces fit together, and how they flow down through an organization's structure, is the core of thinking like a cloud administrator rather than just a cloud user.

sections.heading: Setting the Rules: Azure Policy
sections.body: Azure Policy is the mechanism that answers the question 'what is allowed to happen in this environment, no matter who is asking.' A policy definition is a rule, expressed as a JSON document, that gets evaluated against resources as they are created or updated. Azure ships with a large catalog of ready-made, built-in policy definitions covering everyday needs, such as restricting which Azure regions can be used or requiring that storage accounts encrypt data at rest, so most organizations never need to write a definition from scratch. When a built-in rule doesn't cover something specific to a business, custom policy definitions can be authored to enforce that organization's own requirements. Because real-world compliance needs rarely come as a single rule, related policy definitions are often grouped together into a policy initiative, letting an administrator assign, track, and report on dozens of related rules, such as everything needed to satisfy a particular regulatory standard, as one bundled unit instead of managing each rule individually.

sections.heading: Controlling Access: RBAC and Least Privilege
sections.body: Where Azure Policy governs what can be done regardless of the requester, role-based access control governs who is allowed to do it. RBAC works by assigning a role, such as Owner, Contributor, or Reader, to a user, group, or application at a particular scope, and that assignment determines exactly which actions that identity can perform within that scope. The guiding philosophy behind good RBAC design is the principle of least privilege: every identity should hold only the access it genuinely needs to do its job, and nothing more. A developer who only needs to restart a web app shouldn't also hold the ability to delete the resource group it lives in. Keeping access this tightly scoped isn't about distrust; it's about limiting the damage that a mistake, a compromised account, or a misfiring automation script could cause. It's worth internalizing the distinction clearly: Policy asks 'is this configuration permitted,' while RBAC asks 'is this identity permitted to act here at all.'

sections.heading: Protecting What Matters: Resource Locks
sections.body: Even a well-designed RBAC structure has a gap: an Owner is, by definition, allowed to delete things, which means a single misclick by an authorized, trusted person can still take down a critical resource. Resource locks close that gap by adding a layer of protection that sits above and outside the normal permission system. A lock can be set to prevent deletion outright, or to make a resource read-only so that no property can be changed at all, and critically, a lock applies to everyone touching that resource, including subscription Owners, until the lock itself is removed. Locks are typically reserved for the handful of resources where an accidental change would be genuinely painful to recover from, such as a production database or a shared virtual network, rather than applied blanket-style across an entire environment.

sections.heading: Keeping Things Organized: Tags
sections.body: Not every governance need is about restriction; sometimes the challenge is simply knowing what you have. Tags are key-value labels, such as environment: production or costCenter: marketing, that can be attached to almost any resource, resource group, or subscription. They don't grant or deny any action and they don't get evaluated by Policy or RBAC on their own; their entire purpose is descriptive. Tags make it possible to filter a cost report down to a single department, find every resource that belongs to a particular application, or automate a script that only touches resources marked as non-production. Because tags carry no enforcement power by themselves, they work best alongside a naming convention and, often, a policy that requires certain tags to be present before a resource can even be created.

sections.heading: How It All Cascades: The Governance Hierarchy
sections.body: None of these tools would scale well if they had to be configured separately on every single resource, so Azure organizes everything into a nested hierarchy: a management group can contain multiple subscriptions, each subscription can contain multiple resource groups, and each resource group contains the actual resources. The reason this structure matters for governance is inheritance: a policy assignment or RBAC role granted at a management group automatically applies to every subscription, resource group, and resource nested beneath it, without needing to be reapplied at each level. This lets an organization set broad, non-negotiable rules once at the top, such as blocking deployments outside approved regions, while still allowing individual teams to add further, more specific restrictions lower down for their own resource groups. What a lower scope cannot do is loosen or override a restriction that was inherited from above; the most restrictive applicable rule always wins, which is exactly what keeps top-level governance meaningful.

keyTakeaways: Governance in Azure is achieved through several complementary tools working together, not one single control.
Azure Policy governs what configurations are allowed, regardless of who is making the request.
RBAC governs who can perform which actions, guided by the principle of least privilege.
Resource locks override normal permissions to prevent accidental deletion or modification, even for Owners.
Tags are descriptive metadata only; they carry no enforcement power over access or configuration.
Settings applied at a higher scope, such as a management group, are automatically inherited by everything nested beneath it.
A lower scope can add further restrictions but can never override or loosen a rule inherited from a parent scope.
examTips: AZ-900 governance questions are usually scenario-based: read for the verb. 'Prevent a type of configuration' points to Policy, 'control who can perform an action' points to RBAC, and 'prevent deletion or changes regardless of role' points to Locks.
If a question describes someone with Owner or Contributor access still being unable to delete or modify a resource, the answer is almost always a resource lock, not a missing RBAC assignment.

Expect at least one question that tests inheritance direction directly, such as a rule set at a management group and asking what happens at a subscription beneath it; the answer is that it applies automatically unless a more restrictive rule exists lower down.
Watch for answer choices that claim tags restrict access, enforce compliance, or lock a resource; tags never do any of these, they are purely descriptive.
When a question mentions grouping several related rules under one regulatory or compliance goal, that's describing a policy initiative rather than a single policy definition.

commonMistakes.mistake: If I set someone's role to Reader instead of Contributor, that alone guarantees they can never accidentally break anything important.
commonMistakes.correction: RBAC only controls what a role permits an identity to do; it doesn't create a hard barrier around specific resources. For guaranteed protection of a critical resource against deletion or modification, use a resource lock, since locks apply regardless of anyone's assigned role, including Owners.

commonMistakes.mistake: Tags help keep sensitive resources hidden or restricted from people who shouldn't see them.
commonMistakes.correction: Tags are plain key-value metadata used for organization, cost reporting, and automation. They have no effect whatsoever on who can view, access, or modify a resource; that job belongs to RBAC.

commonMistakes.mistake: Since policy settings flow downward, a team can just set a less restrictive policy on their own resource group to override an inconvenient rule inherited from the management group above.
commonMistakes.correction: Inheritance only flows one direction, from parent scope down to child scope, and it only ever adds restriction, never removes it. When a policy at a lower scope conflicts with one inherited from above, the more restrictive rule always takes effect.

commonMistakes.mistake: Every governance rule a company needs has to be written from scratch as a custom policy.
commonMistakes.correction: Azure provides a large library of built-in policy definitions covering most common scenarios, such as allowed regions or required encryption. Custom policy definitions are only necessary for rules specific to an organization that no built-in definition already covers.

knowledgeCheck.question: A management group has a policy assigned that blocks the creation of virtual machines in any region except West Europe. What happens to the subscriptions nested inside that management group?
options: The restriction applies automatically to those subscriptions unless a more restrictive policy is set lower down
Each subscription owner must manually copy the policy for it to take effect
The policy has no effect until it is individually assigned to every resource group
Only subscriptions created after the policy was assigned are affected
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Policy assignments made at a management group are inherited automatically by every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it in the hierarchy; nothing needs to be manually reapplied at lower scopes.

knowledgeCheck.question: A user holds the Owner role on a resource group, but one resource inside it has a CanNotDelete lock applied. What happens if that user attempts to delete the locked resource?
options: The deletion is blocked, because the lock overrides the permissions granted by the Owner role
The deletion succeeds, because Owner permissions always take priority over locks
The deletion is blocked only if the user is also using a guest account
The lock only affects users with the Reader role, so the Owner can delete it normally
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Resource locks apply regardless of role assignments. A CanNotDelete lock prevents deletion of the resource by anyone, including a user with the Owner role, until the lock itself is removed.

knowledgeCheck.question: A team wants to make sure every storage account it creates is automatically labeled with the department that owns it, so finance reports can be filtered accurately later. Which governance tool is being described, and what does it not do?
options: Tags, which organize and describe resources for reporting but do not restrict what any user can access or do
RBAC roles, which restrict access to only members of that department
Resource locks, which prevent the storage account from being deleted by other departments
Policy initiatives, which enforce the department label as a compliance requirement across the tenant
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Tags are descriptive key-value metadata used for organizing and reporting on resources, such as attributing costs to a department. On their own, tags have no effect on access permissions, deletion protection, or enforcement; those jobs belong to RBAC, locks, and Policy respectively.

monitoring.title: Monitoring

sections.heading: Azure Monitor: The Umbrella for Everything You Run
sections.body: The moment you deploy anything in Azure — a virtual machine, a web app, a database, a virtual network — that resource starts generating a constant stream of information about its own behavior: how busy it is, whether it is responding, what errors it is hitting, who is connecting to it. Left unwatched, that information just evaporates, and you only find out something was wrong when a user complains. Azure Monitor exists to catch that stream before it disappears. It is best thought of not as a single button you press, but as a platform: one collection pipeline that gathers telemetry from almost every Azure service (and, with the right agents, from on-premises and other-cloud machines too), and a shared set of tools built on top of that pipeline for analyzing what it collected and reacting to it. Everything else in this lesson — metrics, logs, Application Insights, alerts, dashboards, workbooks — is a piece of that one platform, not a separate product bolted on beside it. Learning Azure Monitor is really learning how these pieces fit together into a single story: collect, analyze, act.

sections.heading: Metrics and Logs: Two Different Shapes of Telemetry
sections.body: Azure Monitor collects two fundamentally different shapes of data, and confusing them is one of the easiest ways to lose marks or waste time in the real world. A metric is a simple number attached to a timestamp, collected at a regular interval — CPU percentage every minute, the number of requests per second, available memory. Metrics are lightweight and numeric by design, which makes them cheap to collect and fast to plot, so they are what you reach for when you want a near-real-time trend line or a quick chart of 'is this number going up or down.' A log, by contrast, is a record of something that happened, and it can carry far more structure and detail than a single number: a line describing a specific request, an error with its stack trace, a security event, a custom message your own code chose to write out. Logs from across your environment land in a Log Analytics workspace, which is essentially a searchable database purpose-built for this kind of telemetry. To get anything useful out of it you write a query in KQL (Kusto Query Language), a language designed specifically for filtering, joining, and summarizing large volumes of time-stamped log data. The short version: metrics answer 'what is the number right now,' logs answer 'what exactly happened, and why.'

sections.heading: Application Insights: Watching the Code, Not Just the Machine
sections.body: Everything described so far tends to focus on infrastructure — is the VM alive, is the disk full, is the network saturated. But a server can look perfectly healthy while the application running on it is quietly broken: a page that takes eight seconds to load, a dependency call that keeps timing out, an exception being swallowed silently in code. Application Insights is the feature of Azure Monitor built specifically to answer questions at that layer. Once it is enabled for an application — through an SDK added to the code, or increasingly through codeless, agent-based instrumentation — it starts tracking things like incoming requests and how long they take, calls out to dependencies such as databases or external APIs, exceptions thrown, and even how real users are navigating through a web app. This is usually called application performance monitoring, or APM. It is not a competing product to Azure Monitor; it is a specialized lens on the same platform, and the data it collects still lives alongside your other metrics and logs, ready to be queried, alerted on, or charted the same way.

sections.heading: From Signal to Action: Alerts and Action Groups
sections.body: Collecting telemetry is only valuable if something happens when the telemetry looks bad, and this is where alerts come in. An alert rule is a definition of a condition to watch for — evaluated against a metric (CPU above 90 percent for five minutes) or against a log query (more than ten failed sign-ins in the last hour) — plus how often to check it. On its own, though, an alert rule does not know who to tell. That job belongs to a separate resource called an action group: a reusable, named bundle of responses, such as sending an email or SMS, pushing a notification, calling a webhook, running an Azure Automation runbook, invoking a function, or opening a ticket in an ITSM system. The reason these two are kept as separate objects is reusability: a dozen different alert rules across a dozen different resources can all point at the same action group, so when the on-call rotation changes you update one action group instead of hunting down every alert rule that mentions a phone number.

sections.heading: Is Everything Okay? Service Health, Azure Status, and Advisor as Complementary Views
sections.body: Azure Monitor tells you about the behavior of the things you built. It deliberately does not try to answer a different, equally important question: is Azure itself, or my specific corner of it, in good shape right now? Two health-focused tools sit alongside Monitor to cover that ground: Azure Status is a public dashboard showing the health of Azure services globally, visible to anyone, with no awareness of your subscription. Service Health narrows that same kind of information down to what actually matters to you — the specific services and regions your resources depend on — and layers on planned maintenance notices and health advisories tailored to your subscription. A third tool, Azure Advisor, takes a different angle again: rather than reporting live incidents, it periodically reviews your resource configuration and usage patterns and turns that review into personalized, actionable recommendations across cost, security, reliability, performance, and operational excellence. None of these three replace Azure Monitor; they answer 'is everything okay' from angles that raw telemetry dashboards were never designed to cover.

keyTakeaways: Azure Monitor is a platform, not a single feature — Application Insights, Log Analytics, alerts, dashboards, and workbooks are all pieces built on top of one shared collection pipeline.
Metrics are lightweight, numeric, time-stamped values sampled at intervals, ideal for near-real-time trends; logs are richer structured or text records queried with KQL in a Log Analytics workspace.
Application Insights is Azure Monitor's application performance monitoring (APM) feature, focused on request times, dependencies, and exceptions inside your code, not the underlying infrastructure.
An alert rule defines the condition to watch for; an action group defines who or what responds — they are separate resources so one action group can serve many alert rules.
Azure Status is a public, unauthenticated view of global Azure service health, while Service Health is personalized to the resources and regions in your own subscription.
Azure Advisor doesn't collect live telemetry itself — it periodically analyzes your configuration and usage to produce personalized recommendations.
Dashboards, alerts, and workbooks are all downstream consumers of the same metrics and logs that Azure Monitor collects, not separate data sources.
examTips: When a scenario describes a threshold being crossed and someone needing to be paged, look for the pairing of an alert rule (the condition) with an action group (the response) — the exam likes to test that these are two distinct objects.

Scenario questions that say 'I need to know if my application is slow' point to Application Insights; ones that say 'I need to know if Azure itself is having a problem' point to Service Health or Azure Status — read carefully which one is being described.
Keywords are a strong signal: 'near real-time numeric data' or 'trend over time' usually means metrics, while 'searchable,' 'detailed,' or 'query with KQL' usually means logs.
Don't let a question trick you into treating Azure Advisor as a live monitoring tool — it produces recommendations from periodic analysis, it does not stream telemetry like Azure Monitor does.
If a question contrasts 'public/global' information against 'personalized to my subscription,' that phrasing is testing Azure Status versus Service Health specifically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Application Insights and Azure Monitor are two separate, competing monitoring products.
commonMistakes.correction: Application Insights is a feature within Azure Monitor, specialized for application-level telemetry — it shares the same underlying platform and data store, not a rival system.

commonMistakes.mistake: An alert rule already contains the email addresses or phone numbers that get notified.
commonMistakes.correction: The alert rule only defines the condition; the actual notification targets live in a separate, reusable action group that the alert rule points to.

commonMistakes.mistake: Metrics and logs are just two names for the same kind of telemetry.
commonMistakes.correction: They are structurally different — metrics are lightweight numeric time-series values sampled at intervals, while logs are structured or free-text event records analyzed with KQL in a Log Analytics workspace.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking Azure Status will tell me whether my own virtual machine or app is degraded.
commonMistakes.correction: Azure Status is a public, global dashboard with no knowledge of your subscription; Service Health is the tool that scopes health and maintenance information to your actual resources.

commonMistakes.mistake: Azure Advisor continuously watches my resources in real time the way Azure Monitor does.
commonMistakes.correction: Advisor periodically evaluates your configuration and usage data to generate recommendations — it's a review-and-suggest tool, not a live telemetry stream.

A workbook and a dashboard

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Application Insights is the application performance monitoring (APM) feature of Azure Monitor, specifically designed to track request performance, dependencies, and exceptions at the application code level.

pricing.title: Pricing

sections.heading: How Azure Pricing Works
sections.body: Unlike buying a physical server that you own outright regardless of whether it sits idle, Azure charges you based on what you actually consume, and when you consume it. This is called consumption-based billing, and it is the default model for the vast majority of Azure services: pay-as-you-go pricing means you are billed only for the compute hours, storage capacity, or data processed that you actually use, with no long-term contract required to get started. Billing is metered at a fine level of detail, since many services charge per second or per minute rather than rounding up to the nearest hour, so a virtual machine you spin up for twenty minutes to test something costs you for twenty minutes, not a full hour. This flexibility is one of the core value propositions of cloud computing: instead of estimating peak capacity years in advance and buying hardware to match, you scale resources up and down as demand changes and your bill follows along. It also means your monthly invoice can vary from month to month, which is exactly why cost estimation tools and budgeting habits matter so much in Azure, a theme the rest of this lesson builds on.

sections.heading: What Determines the Price of a Resource
sections.body: Not all Azure resources cost the same, and the same resource does not cost the same everywhere or at every size. Three factors combine to determine the price you actually pay, as shown in the diagram below. The first is region: Azure has datacenters spread across the globe, and prices for identical services can differ from one region to another because of local factors like electricity, real estate, and connectivity costs. The second is resource type and tier: choosing a larger virtual machine size, a premium storage tier, or a higher-performance SKU costs more than a basic equivalent, so the pricing tier you select for a service directly shapes your bill. The third is consumption: how many hours a virtual machine runs, how many gigabytes of data you store, how many requests hit an API, or how much data leaves the region all feed into the final number. Understanding that price is a product of where you deploy, what you deploy, and how much you use it helps explain why two people running what sounds like 'the same thing' can see very different invoices.

sections.heading: Estimating Costs Before You Build
sections.body: Azure gives you two distinct tools for reasoning about cost, and knowing which one to reach for is a common source of confusion for newcomers. The Pricing Calculator lets you build out a hypothetical set of resources, say a handful of virtual machines, a database, and some storage, and see an estimated monthly cost for running them on Azure before you provision anything. It is the tool you use when you already know you want to be in Azure and need to answer 'how much will this configuration cost me?' The Total Cost of Ownership, or TCO, Calculator answers a different question: it compares what you are currently spending to run infrastructure on-premises, including easy-to-overlook costs like power, cooling, physical space, and IT labor, against the projected cost of running the equivalent workload in Azure. You would reach for the TCO Calculator when making the business case to migrate to the cloud in the first place, and the Pricing Calculator once you are ready to price out the specific Azure resources that migration would use. Used together, they cover the full journey from 'should we move to the cloud' to 'exactly what will this cost us next month.'

sections.heading: Getting Started for Free
sections.body: Because cost is such a central concern, Microsoft gives newcomers several ways to explore Azure without spending money. Signing up for a free account provides an upfront credit, typically valid for the first 30 days, that you can spend on almost any Azure service while you experiment. On top of that credit, a set of popular services, certain tiers of virtual machines, storage, and databases among them, are free for the first 12 months of the account, letting you build out and run real projects at a small scale without a bill arriving. Separately from both of those time-limited offers, a further list of services is always free, with no time limit and no credit required, for usage under a certain threshold, covering things like a limited number of function executions or a small App Service instance. These three layers, the trial credit, the 12-months-free services, and the always-free services, are easy to conflate, but each has a different scope and expiration, so it is worth being precise about which one applies to a given resource before assuming it will not show up on your invoice.

sections.heading: Support Plans and Licensing Add to Your Bill
sections.body: The cost of running Azure is not limited to the meters on your resources; the level of support you choose and how you license existing software both factor into total spend. Azure support plans come in several tiers, Basic, Developer, Standard, and Professional Direct, and while Basic is included for every subscription at no extra charge, the paid tiers add a recurring monthly fee in exchange for faster response times, deeper technical guidance, and, in the higher tiers, a designated support contact. Choosing a support tier is therefore a genuine cost decision, not just a technical one, and organizations size their choice to how critical their workloads are. Licensing works the other direction: if your organization already owns on-premises licenses for products like Windows Server or SQL Server under Software Assurance, License Mobility lets you bring those existing licenses to Azure instead of paying for new ones, reducing what would otherwise be additional cost baked into the price of a virtual machine or database. Taken together, support and licensing are two of the most commonly overlooked line items when someone first estimates what running a solution on Azure will actually cost.

keyTakeaways: Azure bills primarily on a consumption basis, so cost follows usage rather than upfront hardware purchases.
A resource's price is shaped by three combined factors: region, resource type/tier, and actual consumption.
The Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of a specific Azure configuration, while the TCO Calculator compares on-premises costs to running that workload in Azure.
A free Azure account combines a time-limited trial credit, 12-months-free services, and services that are always free, each with a different scope.
Basic support is included free with every subscription; Developer, Standard, and Professional Direct are paid tiers layered on top.
License Mobility through Software Assurance lets you reuse existing on-premises licenses in Azure instead of buying new ones.
Many services bill in fine-grained increments, such as per-second or per-minute, rather than rounding up to full hours.
examTips: If a question gives you an existing on-premises datacenter's costs and asks about justifying a move to the cloud, that points to the TCO Calculator, not the Pricing Calculator; watch for 'compare current infrastructure costs' language.
Questions about estimating the cost of a proposed set of Azure resources before deploying point to the Pricing Calculator; the giveaway is that no existing on-premises environment is mentioned.

When a scenario mentions region-based price differences or moving a workload to a cheaper region, recognize it is testing the 'region is a pricing factor' concept, not a networking or latency concept.
Support-plan questions often hinge on remembering that Basic is free and included by default; if an option claims all support plans cost extra, it is wrong.

Watch for distractor answers that blend the free account's three tiers together, such as claiming always-free services expire after 12 months; keep the trial credit, 12-months-free, and always-free scopes distinct in your head.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed the Pricing Calculator and the TCO Calculator are basically two names for the same estimating tool.
commonMistakes.correction: They answer different questions: the Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of Azure resources you plan to deploy, while the TCO Calculator compares your current on-premises costs against projected Azure costs to justify migration.

commonMistakes.mistake: I thought everything in my free Azure account stays free forever as long as I don't change any settings.
commonMistakes.correction: Only the always-free tier has no time limit; the signup credit expires after roughly 30 days, and the 12-months-free services stop being free once that year is up, after which normal pay-as-you-go rates apply.

commonMistakes.mistake: I figured picking a cheaper region always means picking one that's geographically closer to me.
commonMistakes.correction: Region pricing is driven by local factors like the cost of power, land, and operations in that datacenter's area, not by physical distance from the customer, so a farther region can sometimes be cheaper.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed Azure support plans are an optional add-on that most subscriptions don't have at all.
commonMistakes.correction: Every Azure subscription automatically includes Basic support at no charge; Developer, Standard, and Professional Direct are the optional paid tiers layered on top of that baseline.

commonMistakes.mistake: I believed License Mobility means Azure gives you free licenses for software you don't already own.
commonMistakes.correction: License Mobility only lets you transfer licenses you already purchased under an existing Software Assurance agreement to Azure; it does not grant new licenses at no cost.

options: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator
Azure Pricing Calculator
Azure Cost Management + Billing
Azure Advisor
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The TCO Calculator is designed specifically to compare the cost of existing on-premises infrastructure against the projected cost of running the equivalent workload in Azure, which is exactly the migration business case described.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three factors that combine to determine the price of an Azure resource?
options: The region where the resource is deployed
The resource type or pricing tier selected
How much of the resource is actually consumed
The programming language used to build the application
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Region, resource type/tier, and consumption are the three factors that determine price. The programming language used in an application has no bearing on the underlying resource's billing.

knowledgeCheck.question: A startup deploys a small App Service instance that stays within Azure's always-free usage limits. What should they expect regarding cost 18 months after creating their account?
options: The service remains free, since always-free offers have no expiration date tied to account age
The service starts billing after 12 months, since all free offers expire after a year
The service starts billing after 30 days, since that is when the trial credit runs out
The service becomes free only if they upgrade to a paid support plan
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Always-free services are distinct from the 30-day trial credit and the 12-months-free tier; as long as usage stays under the specified threshold, they remain free indefinitely regardless of account age.

cost-management.title: Cost Management

sections.heading: Why Cloud Spend Needs a Different Mindset
sections.body: On-premises IT spending is mostly fixed and slow-moving: you buy servers, and the bill doesn't change much month to month whether you use the hardware heavily or let it sit idle. Azure flips that model. Almost everything is billed on consumption, by the minute or by the gigabyte, and because any authorized person on a team can spin up new resources in seconds, spend can grow just as quickly as usage does. That flexibility is a huge advantage, but it also means nobody is naturally forced to stop and ask 'should we be spending this?' the way a hardware purchase order would. Microsoft addresses this gap with a set of tools and practices built around visibility, control, and accountability, so that the same elasticity that makes the cloud powerful doesn't turn into an unpleasant surprise on next month's invoice.

sections.heading: Seeing Where the Money Goes
sections.body: Before an organization can control spend, it needs to understand it, and that visibility starts with Azure Cost Management + Billing, the built-in toolset for tracking every dollar an Azure environment consumes. Billing accounts and invoices tell you what you owe overall, while views like cost analysis let you break that number down: by subscription, by resource group, by service, or by the tags applied to individual resources. Because Azure organizes resources into a hierarchy of scopes, management groups at the top, then subscriptions, then resource groups, cost tools can be pointed at any level of that hierarchy, letting a finance team see an entire department's cloud footprint or a project lead see just their own resource group. Getting comfortable navigating that hierarchy is the first real skill in cost management, because every budget, alert, and export you configure later inherits the scope you choose here.

sections.heading: Budgets and Alerts Working Together
sections.body: Once spend is visible, the next step is setting a guardrail, and that guardrail is a budget: a spending limit defined over a scope and a time period, typically monthly. A budget by itself doesn't do anything active; its value comes from the alerts attached to it. When configuring those alerts, it's worth understanding that they can watch two different numbers. An actual cost alert compares the threshold to money already spent, so it fires only after the line has genuinely been crossed. A forecasted cost alert instead looks at the current spending trend and estimates where that trend is heading, so it can warn you before the period ends that you're on track to blow past the threshold, giving a team time to react rather than just finding out after the fact. Either way, it's important to remember that a budget alert is a notification mechanism, typically an email or an action group, not an enforcement mechanism; Azure won't automatically shut anything down just because a budget was exceeded.

sections.heading: Paying Less for the Same Workloads
sections.body: Alongside monitoring spend, Azure offers several ways to lower the underlying price of the resources you're already using, and each one trades a different kind of commitment for a different kind of discount. Reservations offer the steepest discounts, sometimes up to around 70%, in exchange for committing to a specific resource type, in a specific region, for a one- or three-year term paid upfront or monthly. Azure Savings Plans for Compute take a more flexible approach: instead of locking in one exact VM configuration, you commit to spending a fixed dollar amount per hour, and that commitment automatically applies across whichever eligible compute services, VM families, regions, or operating systems you happen to be running, at the cost of a slightly smaller discount than a matching reservation. Azure Hybrid Benefit works differently again: it doesn't discount usage directly but lets an organization reuse Windows Server or SQL Server licenses it already owns under Software Assurance, cutting the licensing portion out of the Azure bill entirely. Finally, Spot VMs offer some of the cheapest compute available by selling Azure's unused spare capacity, but that low price comes with the risk of eviction with very little warning whenever Azure needs the capacity back, which makes Spot suitable only for workloads that can tolerate interruption.

sections.heading: Keeping Everyone Accountable
sections.body: Cost visibility and discounts only go so far if nobody feels responsible for the numbers, which is where tagging and rightsizing come in. Applying consistent tags, such as department, project, or environment, to every resource means cost analysis can group spend along organizational lines instead of just technical ones, which is what makes showback (reporting a department's cloud spend for awareness) and chargeback (actually re-billing that spend to a department's budget through an internal transaction) possible in the first place. On the optimization side, rightsizing means periodically checking whether a resource's size still matches how it's actually being used, and adjusting it accordingly; Azure Advisor surfaces many of these opportunities automatically by flagging underused VMs or disks. None of these practices work as a one-time exercise: tagging conventions need to be enforced as new resources are created, and recommendations need to be reviewed on an ongoing basis, which is why mature Azure environments treat cost management as a continuous habit rather than a monthly cleanup task.

keyTakeaways: Azure billing is consumption-based, so cost visibility tools matter more than they would in a fixed-cost, on-premises environment.
Azure Cost Management + Billing is the central hub for monitoring, analyzing, and allocating spend across any scope from a resource group up to a management group.
A budget alert can be triggered by actual spend already incurred or by forecasted spend that's projected to exceed the threshold before the period ends.
Budget alerts only notify; they never automatically stop, delete, or lock resources.
Reservations give the deepest discount but require committing to one specific resource type, region, and term.
Azure Savings Plans for Compute trade a fixed hourly spend commitment for flexibility across VM families, regions, and operating systems.
Tags are what make showback and chargeback possible, turning raw spend data into cost that's attributable to a department, project, or environment.
examTips: AZ-900 scenario questions often hide the actual-vs-forecasted distinction in phrasing like 'before the month ends' or 'is trending toward exceeding' — that wording signals a forecasted alert, not an actual one.
Expect at least one question that tests whether you know a budget alert can stop spending; it can't, it only sends a notification.

When a question describes committing to an hourly dollar amount that flexibly covers different VM sizes or regions, that's a Savings Plan, not a Reservation; watch for that flexible-vs-fixed contrast as a common distractor pair.
If a question mentions reusing licenses the organization already owns, the answer is Azure Hybrid Benefit even if the question doesn't use that exact phrase.
Read for the word 'evictable' or 'interrupted' as the giveaway for Spot VM questions, since that's their defining tradeoff versus other discount options.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed a budget alert would automatically stop resources or block new spending once the threshold was hit.
commonMistakes.correction: A budget alert only sends a notification, typically through email or an action group; it never stops, deletes, or blocks anything by itself, so someone (or some automated process) still has to act on the warning.

commonMistakes.mistake: I thought Reservations and Savings Plans were basically two names for the same discount.
commonMistakes.correction: A Reservation locks in a specific resource type, region, and term for the biggest discount, while a Savings Plan commits to an hourly spend amount that flexibly applies across eligible compute services for a somewhat smaller discount.

commonMistakes.mistake: I figured Spot VMs were just a universally cheaper way to run any VM workload.
commonMistakes.correction: Spot VMs are cheap because Azure can evict them with little warning when it needs the capacity back, so they only make sense for interruption-tolerant workloads like batch processing, not for anything that needs to stay running continuously.

commonMistakes.mistake: I assumed showback and chargeback both mean a department actually gets billed for its cloud usage.
commonMistakes.correction: Showback only reports spend for awareness; chargeback goes a step further and moves that cost onto a department's budget through an actual internal transaction.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which term describes an Azure discount model where you commit to spending a fixed dollar amount per hour on compute, and that commitment can automatically apply across eligible VM sizes, regions, and operating systems?
options: Azure Savings Plan for Compute
Azure Reservation
Azure Hybrid Benefit
Spot VM pricing
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Azure Savings Plans for Compute let you commit to an hourly spend amount that flexibly applies across VM families, sizes, regions, and operating systems, unlike a Reservation, which locks in one specific configuration in exchange for a deeper discount.

knowledgeCheck.question: When an Azure budget's spending threshold is crossed and an alert fires, what actually happens to the resources that caused the overage?
options: Nothing is automatically stopped or deleted; the alert only sends a notification
All virtual machines in the budget's scope are automatically deallocated
The subscription is immediately locked from creating new resources
Azure automatically applies a reservation discount to reduce future costs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A budget alert is purely a notification mechanism; it does not automatically stop, deallocate, or lock any resources. A person or an automated remediation workflow still has to act on the warning.

knowledgeCheck.question: An Azure Advisor recommendation suggests resizing a virtual machine to a smaller SKU because its average CPU utilization has stayed below 5% for the past month. Adopting this recommendation is an example of which cost practice?
options: Rightsizing
Reservation purchase
Chargeback
Budget forecasting
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Adjusting a resource's size to match its actual utilization is the definition of rightsizing, and Azure Advisor is one of the main tools that surfaces these opportunities automatically.
